Kazakh Astro Nomads is a student-led team founded by a 16-year-old IB student from Kazakhstan, based in Doha, Qatar. Inspired by previous research into human settlement in Utopia Planitia, we're developing Utopia Explorer, an interactive Mars navigation tool combining NASA data, route planning, and astronaut safety. Our mission is to make Martian exploration safer through science, engineering, and innovation.

From the Great Steppe to the Stars.

details:
Utopia Explorer — Mars EVA Mission Planner

Utopia Explorer is an interactive mission-planning application designed to help future astronauts explore the Martian surface safely and efficiently. Developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, our project focuses on Utopia Planitia, a region in Mars's northern lowlands with evidence of potential subsurface water ice.

What does our project do?

Our application allows users to plan simulated extravehicular activities (EVAs) from a hypothetical Martian habitat. Using an interactive map, astronauts can select scientific exploration destinations, organize waypoints, visualize routes, and calculate mission requirements.

The system estimates round-trip distances, travel times, crew supply requirements, cargo capacity, and rover energy consumption. It also displays terrain elevation profiles and identifies potential operational concerns, such as insufficient battery capacity or exceeding the planned EVA duration.

Rather than simply showing a map of Mars, Utopia Explorer transforms planetary information into an interactive mission-planning experience.

How does it work?

Users begin by exploring Utopia Planitia through NASA-derived orbital imagery and scientific mapping data. They select destinations and configure mission parameters, including travel speed, available EVA time, crew size, equipment, supplies, and rover battery capacity.

The application then calculates mission estimates and presents the results through interactive visualizations, mission summaries, and terrain profiles. Users can modify their plans, compare scenarios, and export mission data in JSON format.

Technologies and scientific resources

We developed Utopia Explorer using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and Plotly.js for interactive visualizations.

Our scientific resources include NASA's Mars Trek, Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) elevation data, USGS planetary geological mapping, and NASA/JPL research into subsurface ice in Utopia Planitia.

AI-assisted coding tools supported the development process, while the project's scientific focus, requirements, design decisions, and testing were guided by our team.

What makes our project creative?

Utopia Explorer connects two important aspects of future Mars exploration: scientific discovery and astronaut survival.

Instead of focusing exclusively on mapping terrain, we combine navigation with practical engineering considerations, including crew logistics, mission duration, equipment requirements, and rover energy management.

The project was inspired by our previous collaborative research into establishing a sustainable settlement in Utopia Planitia. We wanted to take that research beyond a theoretical presentation and transform it into a functional application that people can explore and interact with.

Benefits and intended impact

Our goal is to demonstrate how planetary data and engineering calculations can support safer, more informed exploration decisions.

The application helps users understand the trade-offs between scientific objectives, travel distance, available resources, and mission constraints. It also provides an educational platform for students interested in planetary science, aerospace engineering, software development, and future human missions to Mars.

Engineering considerations and limitations

Throughout development, we considered terrain conditions, travel distance, EVA duration, resource availability, rover battery capacity, and the importance of returning safely to the habitat.

We also recognize the limitations of available data. Regional elevation maps cannot identify every local obstacle, and our routes are conceptual rather than verified safe paths. Habitat locations, scientific waypoints, and mission parameters are hypothetical. The application is therefore an educational engineering simulation, not an operational navigation system.

Our vision is to make Martian exploration more understandable, interactive, and safety-conscious by bringing together planetary science, software engineering, and practical mission planning.

From the Great Steppe to the Stars.
